title: Good Christian Men, Rejoice
description: John Mason Neale's carol sung to the old German melody In dulci jubilo with Robert Lucas de Pearsall's four-part harmony, as The Cowley Carol Book (1912) prints it, for 2 to 4 singers. This is the UK version: the tune in its steady 3/4 form under Pearsall's chords, where the US version sings the lilting 6/8 form with its cries of "News! News!". All three verses, in F.

credits.tune: "In dulci jubilo", an old German carol tune, as The Cowley Carol Book (1912) prints it
credits.arrangement: Robert Lucas de Pearsall's four parts (The Cowley Carol Book, 1912), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: John Mason Neale died 1866; his three verses as first printed, in Carols for Christmas-tide (1853), read from its Condensed Vocal Parts (1854), the long s modernised, the same words our US version sings, without the cries "News! News!", "Joy! Joy!" and "Peace Peace!", for which this form of the tune has no notes (it is the form the German words "In dulci jubilo" were written for; Neale wrote his for the 6/8 form with the cries)
licence.tune: public domain: the German melody "In dulci jubilo" (The Cowley Carol Book: "XIV Cent. Melody"), as printed there with Pearsall's harmony; the book's editor, George Ratcliffe Woodward, died 1934
licence.arrangement: Robert Lucas de Pearsall's four parts, headed "harmonized by R. L. de Pearsall" in The Cowley Carol Book (Pearsall died 1856; public domain): his tune, key, bass and most of his chords, with Neale's words fitted and the lower parts revoiced for 2 to 4 beginners (bars counted from the first full bar). The words fit the tune as Cowley prints it without a new pitch: the dotted minim A of "won-der" (bar 11) and of "yon-der" (bar 19) is sung as a minim and a crotchet, for "what we", "end-less" and "fear the", and "fore him", "heav'n-ly" and "calls you"; "say:", "bliss;" and "grave:" hold the F through the crotchet "Li'th" ending bar 12, leaving out that chord as Cowley itself does in its fourth verse ("In ver. 4 omit this chord"), and "day:", "this!" and "save!" hold the A through the crotchet "Like" ending bar 16 in the same way, leaving out Pearsall's D minor chord there; the slurred F, G, A on the "o" of "praesepio" and "gremio" (bars 15 and 16, 23 and 24) take a syllable each ("born to-day", "man-ger now"); the last line's first "day!" keeps Cowley's slur from F up to C (bars 27 and 28). Under the tune's slurred C, D, C on "joice" and "voice" the parts move with Pearsall over his F pedal (alto F4, E4, tenor B-flat 3, G3: his B-flat and C chords), sung on the held syllable; his passing quavers (the alto's E under "men," and "soul,", the tenor's D under "Christ" and "in") and the tenor's B-flat under the held "day!" of the last line but one become one note. The alto takes the chord's third: A4 under "joice" and "voice" (his C4, an octave under the tune), with the tenor on C4 (his A3); A4 on "Give" and F4 on "ye" (his F4 on "ye"), and E4 on "Ox", so that chord is A minor (his F over A, alto F4), then D4 on "and" (his F4), so the alto and bass don't move in fifths; E4 on "to" and "be-" under the tune's B-flat (his G4), the tenor taking the G (his E3); D4 on "bow," (his F4, in unison with the tune, the note he gives the alto in bar 12); A3 on "And" (his F4, in unison), the tenor on F3 (his A3); B-flat 3 then D4 on "Je-sus" and "He is" (his F4, a second under the tune's G), the tenor on F3 (his D4); A3, B-flat 3, C4 on "born to-day:" and "man-ger now." (his F4 three times, in unison with the tune, a second under it, then a third), the tenor on F3, F3, A3 (his A3, B-flat 3, C4); A3 on the last line but one's "Christ is" (his D4, in unison with the tune's low D), the tenor on F3 (his A3), then C sharp 4, held, on "born to-" (his D4 and C sharp 4: the B-flat 3 before it made an augmented second) (his D4, a second under the tune's E, and C sharp 4) and D4 on "day!"; in the last line B-flat 3 on "born to-" (his F4, a second under the tune's G, and E4), so the chord before the end is C7 (his C), and A3 on the last "day!" (his C4, a bare fourth under the tune), the tenor singing F3, F3, G3, E3 (his F3, B-flat 3, D4, C4). The tenor's last note is C3 in verse 3, so the last chord is complete, and F3 in verses 1 and 2 (his A3), leading into the next verse; the tenor sings F3 under "day!" in the last line but one (his A3), so tenor and bass don't move in fifths into the C chord. The bass is Pearsall's throughout, his held F pedal sung once a syllable. Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last note gives up three quarters of a beat (a whole beat after "voice;" and "now.", "more.", "hall:"), the song's last note held. Accepted exceptions: the duet sings Pearsall's bare fourth (F over C) on the crotchets "Good", "ian" and "and", his bare fifth (C over F) on "With", and his fourth (B-flat over F) on the last line's "is", all weak beats, and a fourth on "sus" and "is" (G over D) and an octave on "ye" and "and" (D), weak beats too; on the last line but one's "Christ is" the duet sings a bare fourth (D over A) for three beats, as the tune lies low and the alto can't take the F under it (the trio and quartet are D minor); on "born" there the duet and trio have E and B-flat without the G, which the tenor sings, and on the last line's "to-" the C7 has its third only in the tenor; the alto and bass move with the tune's slur under "voice", and the alto, tenor and bass under the last line but one's "day!", where Pearsall's chord changes; the alto keeps his leap from C4 up to F4 on "men," and "soul," (then D4), and leaps D4 up to A4 on "joice" and "voice", turning back by a fourth to E4 under "voice"; fewer than 70% of the alto's and tenor's moves are steps (Pearsall's lines move by thirds and fourths over his pedal); the key's leading tone E is doubled by the tune and bass on "born to-" in the last line but one (Pearsall's chords there); the alto and bass move in octaves (D to B-flat) across the breath into "Je-sus", and the tune and tenor (A to C) across the breath into "Ox". The tenor holds F3 from "say:" (and "bliss;", "grave:") into "Je-sus" (his A3), so tenor and bass don't move in fifths there. The alto and bass move in contrary fifths (C4 over F3 to E4 over A2) across the breath into "Ox".
licence.source: The Cowley Carol Book for Christmas, Easter, and Ascension-tide, compiled and arranged by the Rev. G. R. Woodward, M.A., Revised and Enlarged Edition (London: A. R. Mowbray & Co. Ltd., 28 Margaret Street, Oxford Circus, W.; Oxford: 9 High Street; 1912), No. 12, second tune, "In Dulci Iubilo", p. 22, headed "The same as preceding, harmonized by R. L. de Pearsall.", in four parts on two staves in F major, 3/4, with a crotchet pickup, written here in F in 3/4 as printed; read from the scan at archive.org/details/cowleycarolbook0000grwo/page/n31 (the first tune, Bach's harmony, is on p. 20, which gives the melody as "XIV Cent. Melody"). Cowley prints Woodward's macaronic words ("In dulci iubilo, Now sing we all io"), not Neale's, which are fitted to its tune as set out under the arrangement. Neale's words read from The Condensed Vocal Parts to the Carols for Christmas-tide; set to Ancient Melodies by the Rev. T. Helmore, M.A.; the Words, principally in imitation of the original, by the Rev. J. M. Neale, M.A. (London: J. Alfred Novello, 1854), No. VI, "Good Christian men, rejoice.", pp. 20 and 21, at commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Condensed_Vocal_Parts_to_the_Carols_for_Christmas-tide.pdf (PDF pages 26 and 27); every word as our US version sings it, "before him bow" and "Peace Peace!" as printed there, the cries left out here. Pearsall's own setting of "In dulci jubilo", for eight solo voices and chorus, was first printed by D'Almaine & Co., London, its cover dated 1836 and Pearsall's preface 31 January 1837 (IMSLP's publisher information for its scan #887185, at imslp.org/wiki/In_dulci_jubilo_(Pearsall,_Robert_Lucas); the score itself not opened); W. J. Westbrook's four-voice reduction (Novello's Part-Song Book, second series, No. 296, London: Novello, Ewer and Co., undated), which says it keeps "the composer's parts with as little alteration as possible", opens with the same tune and chords as Cowley (its pp. 82 and 83 seen at archive.org/details/imslp-dulci-jubilo-pearsall-robert-lucas)
